advisor.summary: §1400Z-2 lets a taxpayer defer an eligible capital gain by reinvesting it in a Qualified Opportunity Fund within 180 days and — the durable prize — steps the QOF interest's basis to fair market value after a ten-year hold, removing all post-investment appreciation from federal tax. The regime boundary dominates 2026 planning: original-regime deferrals end December 31, 2026, while OBBBA's permanent 'OZ 2.0' governs investments made on or after January 1, 2027, with a rolling five-year deferral, a basis step-up for five-year holds (enhanced for rural funds), and refreshed zone maps. For gains realized in 2026, placing the 180-day window on the right side of that boundary is the central move. The engine models only the deferral — it removes the invested gain from the current year's long-term gain — and deliberately leaves the ten-year exclusion unquantified, since it turns on growth no one can forecast.
mechanics: Only the gain — never the full proceeds — needs to move: an eligible capital gain reinvested in a QOF within 180 days of recognition defers under §1400Z-2, and Reg. §1.1400Z2(a)-1 lets K-1 gains start the window at the entity's year-end.
Original-regime investments recognize the deferred gain at the earlier of an inclusion event or December 31, 2026 — a 2026 gain invested under the old rules buys months of deferral, not years.

For investments made on or after January 1, 2027, P.L. 119-21 delivers a rolling five-year deferral, a basis step-up for gains held the full five years (larger for qualified rural funds), recurring zone redesignations, and the same ten-year fair-market-value step-up.
Funds self-certify on Form 8996 and must hold 90% of assets in qualified opportunity zone property; investors report holdings, deferrals, and inclusion events each year on Form 8997.
The model removes the invested gain from the current year's long-term capital gain and stops there — the deferred gain's later inclusion and the ten-year exclusion sit outside the single-year engine.

authority.note: Governs deferral of reinvested gains, inclusion events, and the ten-year step-up of basis to fair market value.
OZ 2.0 beginning 2027: rolling five-year deferral, five-year basis step-up with a rural enhancement, and recurring zone designations; original-regime deferrals still terminate December 31, 2026.
The zone-designation framework that defines the investment universe.
180-day window mechanics, including the flexible start dates available for K-1 gains.
The investor's annual report of QOF holdings, deferrals, and inclusion events.
QOF self-certification and the 90% qualified-property asset test the fund must pass year after year.

requirements: An eligible capital gain with its 180-day clock mapped precisely — K-1 start-date options included — before any money moves.
A diligenced fund: sponsor track record, 90%-test history, and rural-fund status wherever the enhanced step-up is in play.
Liquidity to pay the tax when the deferred gain returns, because no sale proceeds arrive with the inclusion.
A genuine ten-year horizon — as a pure deferral play, the strategy is weak.
risks: The leading 2026 hazard is the regime boundary itself: a gain invested a few weeks early lands in the old regime and is recognized at December 31, 2026, while the same gain invested after January 1, 2027 (where the 180-day window permits) captures the five-year deferral — a calendar error with a six-figure cost and no after-the-fact cure.
Phantom income at the inclusion date: many funds distribute nothing when the tax comes due — the liquidity plan is part of the strategy, not an afterthought.
Investment risk outweighs the tax benefit: a weak fund loses more principal than the deferral saves, and the adviser's job is the tax mechanics, not the underwriting.
Fund-level failures of the 90% test generate penalties and can put investor benefits at risk.
The deferred gain comes back at future rates — rate risk cuts both ways.
stateNotes: Conformity is genuinely mixed: several states never conformed to the §1400Z-2 deferral or exclusion, so state tax may be due currently even while the federal gain defers — screen every state in the footprint before wiring.
Missouri conforms via its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121), so both the federal deferral and the exclusion flow into the Missouri computation.
PTET interaction: ordinarily none — the gain defers at the owner level; a PTET issue arises only if an electing entity itself realizes and reinvests the gain.
reviewChecklist: 180-day window computed and documented — including any K-1 start-date election — against the 2026/2027 regime boundary.
Fund diligence file complete: Form 8996 history, 90% test, sponsor record, and rural status if claimed.
Client's liquidity plan for the inclusion-date tax reviewed and documented.
State conformity screened for every state in the filing footprint.
Form 8997 calendared each year and the ten-year anniversary docketed.

client.teaser: Reinvest a large gain, put off the tax, and let the new growth become tax-free.
client.headline: Turn one big gain into tax-free growth
plainEnglish: Sell something at a big profit — stock, a business, real estate — and the tax normally comes due that year. Opportunity Zone rules open another path. Put the profit into a special fund within 180 days, and the tax waits for years.

The bigger prize comes later. Hold the fund ten years, and all its growth can be sold free of federal tax. The original tax still comes due at a set point. But everything earned on top can escape tax completely.

Timing matters a lot right now. The old program ends December 31, 2026. A better, permanent version starts January 1, 2027, with a five-year delay on the tax. For gains this year, a few weeks can decide which rules you get. We manage that calendar.
client.analogy: It is like replanting the profit from one harvest in fresh soil — wait ten seasons, and all that grows from it is yours to keep.
